title: Ponsonby's New Radiology Service offering High Quality, Precise Ultrasound and X-Ray Services
summary: LUX Radiology is a boutique medical imaging group offering high-quality ultrasound and X-ray services across two clinics in Ponsonby.

children.text: LUX Radiology is a boutique medical imaging group offering high-quality ultrasound and X-ray services in Ponsonby.
Proudly locally-owned and operated, we aim to deliver a professional yet friendly experience for our patients and their referring practitioners.

LUX was the brainchild of two local urgent care doctors, who wanted to provide an on-site radiological service for their patients, in order to create a one-stop, complementary service for patients needing imaging services in a timely fashion, ideally within the same visit to the medical clinic.

LUX means 'light' in Latin, and this name was chosen for the clinic as radiological imaging, be it X-Ray, Ultrasound, CT or MRI scanning, gives light to darkness; where was once uncertainty about a patient's medical or injury diagnosis, radiology can shed light and aid doctors in making an accurate diagnosis, therefore providing the appropriate treatment.

Our company logo was inspired by the Aurora Australis photos taken on an Air New Zealand flight over the Southern Ocean towards the Antarctica. Also known as the Southern Lights, this is a spectacular and magical phenomena - the LUX logo simulates the constantly shifting waves and colours of this beautiful light, echoing our aim to provide beautiful radiological images for accuracy of diagnosis; and, for maternity ultrasound, images that mothers-to-be can also share.
Our first clinic in central Ponsonby started up right in the middle of the first nationwide Covid19 lockdown in August 2020.
We started with general and maternity ultrasound, and have since expanded to include X-ray, 3D/4D maternity bonding scans, and a top-class interventional musculoskeletal ultrasound service.
Meet Alan McNair, our experienced & friendly Radiographer.

Alan is the proud operator of our brand new, state of the art Siemens X-ray machine. He comes with many years' experience in medical imaging, having worked in various radiological practices in New Zealand over the past 30 years. He is meticulous in his work, providing precise, high quality X-ray images to help with accurate diagnosis of a patient's injury or medical condition.

Patients may book online, by phone or walk-in for X-ray services. As this service is based in a medical clinic with casting and splinting services, patients may choose to have their treatment started at the clinic (if required) after the X-ray, and are referred back to their doctor for follow up.
Meet Andrew Graham, our MusculoSkeletal Ultrasound Expert.

Andrew is highly experienced and unique in his field, as he holds both Physiotherapy and Sonography qualifications. He is particularly skilled in MSK scanning and injection therapy, including steroid and barbotage. These interventions can be very effective for painful, injured or arthritic joints, allowing the patient to walk out pain-free with a smile on their face, and restoring their joint functionality and quality of life.

Referrals are required from your GP or specialist for injection therapies, or make an appointment to see one of our doctors in the clinic to ascertain your suitability for treatment. Andrew has a good relationship with a team of orthopaedic surgeons and physiotherapists, and can guide you on the next steps following your treatment.
Introducing Ginny, our Maternity Ultrasound Superstar.

Ginny has 20 years experience working in public and private practices throughout New Zealand. She has a passion for maternity and gynaecology ultrasound, and is also highly skilled in vein mapping. Patients rave about her thoroughness, warmth and friendliness.

She now offers an exclusive 3D/4D pregnancy scan service. 3D ultrasounds create a three-dimensional image of your baby, while 4D ultrasounds create a live video effect, like a movie - you can watch your baby smile or yawn. This provides a special bonding experience for parents, family, and friends - a truly special moment indeed! Also included are photos and videos of the scan to share with your loved ones.

This scan is best performed between 28 and 32 weeks for best views of the baby. You can purchase this experience for yourself, or as a gift for a mom-to-be. Gift certificates are available on our website, and we can email this to your giftee along with a special message from yourself.
About the clinics: LUX Radiology operates at 582 Karangahape Rd ( Inside the Ponsonby Doctors Clinic ).

A wide range of ultrasound services are offered in both locations. 3D/4D scans are offered at the Ponsonby Road clinic; MSK ultrasounds and joint injections at the K Rd clinic. X-ray is based at the K Road clinic.
Ultrasound services are appointment-based; while for X-ray, bookings and walk-ins are accepted.
LUX will be open on most days during the Christmas and New Year's period.
The LUX team look forward to meeting you and caring for our local Ponsonby community and beyond.

title: Ultrasound Imaging
shortDescription: Ultrasound is the term used for high frequency soundwaves. An ultrasound examination uses these sound waves to produce an image onto a screen that shows the inside of your body.

children.text: Ultrasound scans use high-frequency sound waves to make images of organs and structures inside the body.
They allow doctors to see more clearly what is happening inside of your body, analyse injuries and diagnose disease in a safe and non-invasive way.
Learn more about Ultrasound imaging
An overview of ultrasound techniques and results

Ultrasound (also known as sonography or sonogram) is the term used for high frequency soundwaves. An ultrasound examination uses this sound wave technology to produce an image onto a screen that shows the inside of your body.
What is an ultrasound?

An ultrasound examination is performed using a smooth, hand held device called a transducer (camera) that is move across the body with a sliding and rotating action. The transducer transmits the high-frequency sound waves into your body. The sound waves are then reflected from the different tissues in different ways. The sound waves are converted to electrical impulses, which are used to produce a moving image onto the screen.
Why would my doctor refer me for an ultrasound appointment?

An ultrasound examination is often used in medical care during pregnancy and childbirth. It is an ideal examination to look at the baby as it grows throughout the various stages of pregnancy, and is a wonderful opportunity to meet your forming baby.

Ultrasound can take high quality pictures or images of most parts of your body, which makes it an excellent diagnostic test. For example, it is used to examine abdominal and other organs, to watch blood flow in any of the arteries or veins throughout the various parts of your body, and to evaluate the musculoskeletal system (muscles, bones and joints related).
Ultrasound examinations are used to evaluate many superficial structures in your body such as breast, and in children special areas such as newborn hips, spine and brain.
How do I prepare for ultrasound services?
Read any instructions given to you by your doctor, or provided by us
Wear clothing that will provide easy access to the area that is being imaged
Bring any previous ultrasound examination films with you, for comparison.

IMPORTANT: If you have diabetes, or you are on any medications prescribed by your doctor, or any other medication including any over the counter medicines or complementary therapies such as vitamins, etc., contact us to check special preparation instructions.

Preparation depends on the type of ultrasound examination you are having. The following is a guide for the most common examinations, it may vary slightly depending on the clinic you attend but we will confirm details when you make your appointment.
Gallbladder or upper abdomen
Please prepare as follows;
Nothing to eat 6 hours prior to your scan and only water to drink. If you are diabetic, please consult with your Doctor.
Continue taking your medication as normal.
Renal, kidney, bladder, prostate, lower abdomen, female pelvic ultrasound, gynae, or dating pregnancy ultrasounds
Please prepare as follows;
Please arrive to your scan with a full bladder. Empty your bladder one hour prior then drink 3-4 glasses of water,
If your bladder is not full ten minutes prior to your examination, please drink more water. If you are uncomfortably full you may let some out.
Abdomen or pelvis
Please prepare as follows;
Nothing to eat 6 hours prior to your scan and only water to drink. If you are diabetic, please consult with your Doctor.
Continue taking your medication as normal.
Please arrive to your scan with a full bladder. Empty your bladder one hour prior then drink 3-4 glasses of water,
If your bladder is not full ten minutes prior to your examination, please drink more water. If you are uncomfortably full you may let some out.
Other examination areas
For all other areas, no preparation required.
What happens during an ultrasound?

Before you have the examination, the sonographer (technologist), will ask you questions about why you have come for the ultrasound scan. They will then explain the procedure you are having in detail and answer any questions you have.

You are normally asked to lie down on a bed and the area to be examined is exposed while the rest of the body is covered. If your examination is in the pelvic or abdomen area, you will be given a sheet to cover yourself with to maintain your privacy. You will be asked to move the sheet aside to allow the sonographer to carry out the examination.

Clear gel is applied to the area of your body which is being imaged. The sonographer will then place the transducer (camera) onto this area using gentle pressure. The transducer is moved across the area with a sliding and rotating action to allow the image to project onto the screen.

The sonographer takes still photographs from the moving images on the screen. During the examination you may be asked to perform some simple movements to improve the quality of the imaging. These movements you will be asked to perform will be simple, for example:
‘Taking a bigger breath’ to assist during an abdominal ultrasound and allow the areas underneath the rib cage to be clearly viewed
During an obstetric examination you may be asked to roll around to encourage the foetus or unborn baby to roll into a position appropriate for imaging
In musculoskeletal ultrasound, the transducer moving over any painful areas often provides valuable insights into the true source of the pain
However, if any of these movements cause you concern or discomfort, you should let the sonographer know immediately.
How long does an ultrasound take?

Typically, an ultrasound examination will take about 30 minutes. However, some examinations, may take longer than this because of the detailed imaging that is required and the number and size of the organ/s being examined. Ask us when making your appointment how long the type of ultrasound you are having normally takes.
What are the benefits of ultrasound?
Ultrasound provides excellent imaging of the soft tissues of the human body and is often the best and most appropriate diagnostic test.

It is a safe procedure which does not have the risks associated with imaging that uses radiation. There are no proven harmful effects of sound waves at the levels used in ultrasound performed in our clinics.

Ultrasound can be performed with patient movement so is ideal for imaging babies and children. Imaging movement is also very valuable in musculoskeletal (muscles, bones and joints related), gynaecological (women’s health, especially of the reproductive organs) and vascular (blood vessel related) ultrasound. Dynamic imaging (moving pictures) provided by images using ultrasound sound waves gives the opportunity for looking at the inside of the body in positions or with movements where there is pain or movement restriction.

Ultrasound does not require an injection of contrast medium (a small amount of material used with some X-ray scanning to detect certain types of diseases or problems in the body). Ultrasound is mostly non-invasive, provides accurate imaging tests of the human body, is readily available and relatively inexpensive.
Who does an ultrasound?

The ultrasound examination is performed by a sonographer, a health professional specialised in performing ultrasound examinations. They have a graduate qualification and are fully qualified to perform the examination.

The sonographer performs the examination and provides an interpretation of the images on the screen to a radiologist (medical specialist), who will review the sonographer’s interpretation and discuss the images with them, before providing a report on the findings to your doctor.
What are the risks of an ultrasound?
Ultrasound is a safe examination which provides excellent imaging without any significant risk.
Are there any after effects of an ultrasound?
It is rare to have after effects from an ultrasound examination.
How do I get my results?

Your doctor will receive a written report on your test as soon as is practicable. It is very important that you discuss the results with the doctor whom referred you so that they can explain what the results mean for you.

Learn more about X-Ray imaging
Radiography is the imaging of body structures using X-Rays, which are a form of radiation similar to visible light, radiowaves and microwaves.
What is a general or plain X-Ray?

Radiography is the imaging of body structures using X-Rays, which are a form of radiation similar to visible light, radiowaves and microwaves. X-radiation is special because it has a very high energy level that allows the x-ray beam to penetrate through the body and create an image or picture.

The image is created due to the x-ray beam being absorbed differently by different structures or parts in the body. A dense structure like bone absorbs a high percentage of the X-Ray beam (which appears light grey on the image), while low density structures like soft tissues absorb a small percentage (which appears dark grey on the image). The body has many different structures of varying densities and this difference creates a picture or image.
What happens during a plain X-Ray radiographic service?
The radiographer (a trained x-ray technologist) will call your name and escort you through to an examination room. They will explain the procedure and prepare you accordingly.

Depending on the part of your body being examined you may be asked to stand, sit or lie down while the X-Ray is taken. The number of x-rays taken and the speed of the test will also depend on this. It is important that you stay completely still when the radiographer instructs you to, as any movement may create a blurred image.

After the X-Rays have been performed, the radiographer has to process each X-Ray and check the results for quality. This can sometimes take several minutes. Sometimes there will be a need for additional images to be taken to obtain more information to help the radiologist (a specialist doctor) make a diagnosis. There is no need for concern if this happens as it is quite common.

The radiographer will instruct you when the procedure is finished. The radiologist then carefully assesses the images, makes a diagnosis and produces a written report on the findings, which is sent to your referring doctor.
The entire process is straightforward and you will not feel anything strange or feel any different during the examination. You are welcome to ask questions at any stage.
How do I prepare for a plain X-Ray appointment?

For a plain X-Ray there are no specific preparation instructions. You must however bring the X-Ray request form or referral letter from your doctor, as no X-Ray examination can be performed without it.

Please inform the radiographer who is performing the X-Ray if there is any chance you may be pregnant. Safety of the patient and unborn child is the number one priority so a different approach or test may be needed. As some clothing can make it difficult to see the images clearly, be prepared to wear a gown.
Be prepared to remove certain items like watches, necklaces and certain types of clothing that contain metal objects such as zips, as these items may interfere with the quality of the image.
Who does plain X-Rays?

A radiographer or medical imaging technologist is a health professional who performs diagnostic radiography. A radiologist is a specialist medical doctor who reviews and interprets the images and provides a written report of the test to your referring doctor.
How long do plain X-Ray radiology services take?
The radiographer (a trained X-Ray technologist) will call your name and escort you through to an examination room. They will explain the procedure and prepare you accordingly.

Depending on the part of your body being examined you may be asked to stand, sit or lie down while the X-Ray is taken. The number of X-Rays taken and the speed of the test will also depend on this. It is important that you stay completely still when the radiographer instructs you to, as any movement may create a blurred image.

After the X-Rays have been performed, the radiographer has to process each X-Ray and check the results for quality. This can sometimes take several minutes. Sometimes there will be a need for additional images to be taken to obtain more information to help the radiologist (a specialist doctor) make a diagnosis. There is no need for concern if this happens as it is quite common.

The radiographer will instruct you when the procedure is finished. The radiologist then carefully assesses the images, makes a diagnosis and produces a written report on the findings, which is sent to your referring doctor.
The entire process is straightforward and you will not feel anything strange or feel any different during the examination. You are welcome to ask questions at any stage.
What are the risks of plain X-Rays?

Generally, the benefit of the X-Ray procedure is far more important than the small estimated risk. At the radiation dose levels that are used in diagnostic radiography there is little or no evidence of health effects.
The two major risks to health that occur as a result of exposure to medical ionizing radiation (which is the kind of radiation in X-Rays) are:
Cancer occurring many years after the radiation exposure
Health problems in the children born to people exposed to radiation because of damage to the reproductive cells in the body.

To put this into perspective, a patient would need to have approximately 38 chest X-Rays to receive an amount of radiation similar to that of normal background radiation that everyone receives for one year from the environment.
How do I get my results?
Your doctor will receive a written report on your test as soon as is practicable.
It is very important that you discuss the results with the doctor whom referred you so that they can explain what the results mean for you.

title: Earth Sun
brief:
I am writing to express my concern and dissatisfaction regarding an ultrasound I underwent at your clinic on 6th June.
The report I received stated that I had two significantly enlarged lymph nodes, measuring approximately 50mm in diameter. Naturally, this finding was extremely alarming and caused me significant emotional distress. Based on this report, I promptly sought further medical advice from a specialist, which involved another ultrasound and consultation—costing me nearly $1000 in total.
However, the specialist’s ultrasound revealed that the lymph nodes were not nearly as large as your report had indicated. The discrepancy between the two results was substantial. Furthermore, I noticed a marked difference in the clarity and resolution between your imaging equipment and the specialist’s. Their equipment provided a much more precise and reliable image.
I believe this issue may have resulted from a combination of inaccurate measurement by the sonographer and limitations in the quality of your ultrasound machine. Had your clinic provided accurate results in the first place, I would not have endured unnecessary stress or incurred additional expenses.
I am writing this not only to raise a complaint but also to warn other patients who may be considering getting their scans done at Lux. If patients are paying similar fees, they deserve the assurance of accurate diagnostics and modern equipment—not the risk of being misled by substandard imaging and imprecise evaluations.

title: Willa
brief:
I recently had a deeply unsatisfactory experience at Lux Radiology, primarily due to the unprofessional conduct and inadequate service of their reception staff. Despite my insurance company having directly paid the required amount to Lux Radiology’s account, the staff insisted that I immediately find and provide email proof of the transaction. This was incredibly frustrating, especially considering I am capable of making a payment and resolving it with the insurance company later if necessary.

What was particularly disheartening was the refusal of the reception staff to verify the payment, despite having enough personnel available to handle such a query. The reception area was not excessively busy at the time, which made their reluctance even more baffling. This raises serious concerns about the professionalism and attitude of the staff.

I was treated rudely because I couldn’t immediately find the proof of payment among my many emails (personal, university-related, etc.). Even though the insurance company confirmed over the phone that they would handle the follow-up, the staff still forced me to pay on the spot and resolve it with the insurance company later. While I understood this resolution, I was infuriated by the unfriendly manner in which the staff handled the situation.

Moreover, I was shocked to see the reception staff dressed inappropriately for a medical clinic, wearing sandals and extremely short skirts. This lack of professional attire and their behavior—leaning against the door and chatting and laughing until rudely calling me back to inform me I hadn’t paid—made me question the clinic’s understanding of professional service standards. Despite having four or five staff members at the reception, they couldn’t manage to check a simple $425 payment, leaving me to stand at the front desk and negotiate with the insurance company for 18 minutes, only to end up paying again.

Today’s experience was deeply unsatisfactory. It was not a matter of the payment itself but rather the apparent unwillingness and inability of your staff to efficiently manage and address my concern. I am appalled by the lack of basic customer service and the overall dismissive attitude displayed.

While Andrew, the technician who performed my examination, was commendable in his duties, the same cannot be said for your reception staff. Their behavior left me questioning the internal training and management practices at Lux Radiology. The rude and unprofessional conduct severely impacted my perception of the clinic’s quality of care.

I regret to say that I will no longer be utilizing Lux Radiology’s services for any future medical examinations. I hope that the management takes this feedback seriously and implements necessary changes to prevent such incidents from recurring. The staff’s inability to handle simple tasks and their preference for idle conversation over assisting clients is both laughable and unacceptable. This experience has been nothing short of a nightmare, and I would not recommend Lux Radiology to anyone seeking professional and courteous medical services.

During weeks 36 and 37, the baby’s organs are fully developed and ready for birth. The baby practices sucking and swallowing, essential skills for feeding after birth. The baby may start to drop lower into the pelvis, a process known as lightening, which can make breathing easier for the mother.

In the 40th week, the baby is fully developed and ready for birth. The average weight is between 6-9 pounds, and the baby may be born any day now. The mother and baby have completed a remarkable journey of growth and development, and they are both prepared for the exciting moment of birth.
The baby is fully developed and ready for birth.

In weeks 38 and 39, the baby’s brain and lungs continue to mature, preparing for life outside the womb. The baby’s movements may decrease as it has less space to move, but it is still active. The baby’s skin is smooth and has a healthy pink color, indicating good blood circulation and overall health.
The baby’s brain and lungs continue to mature.

In weeks 34 and 35, the baby's lungs are almost fully developed and ready for breathing air. The baby starts to move into a head-down position in preparation for birth, making it easier to navigate the birth canal. The baby continues to gain weight, providing more energy reserves for the journey ahead.

In weeks 30 and 31, the baby’s brain continues to grow and develop, forming more complex neural connections. The baby starts to shed the lanugo hair that has been covering its body. The baby practices breathing movements more frequently, preparing the lungs for breathing air after birth.
The baby’s brain continues to grow and develop.

During weeks 32 and 33, the baby’s skin becomes less wrinkled as fat continues to accumulate, providing more insulation and energy reserves. The baby starts to develop a more regular sleep-wake cycle, with periods of activity and rest. The baby’s movements may start to slow down as it runs out of space in the womb.

During weeks 28 and 29, the baby can open and close its eyes, and the baby continues to gain weight rapidly. The bones are fully developed but still soft and pliable, allowing for easier passage through the birth canal. The baby is preparing for the final stages of development and birth.
The baby can open and close its eyes.
The baby continues to gain weight rapidly.
The bones are fully developed but still soft.

In the 27th week, the baby's eyes begin to open, and the baby can detect changes in light and dark. The lungs continue to develop and practice breathing movements, although they are not yet fully ready for breathing air. The baby is becoming more aware of its surroundings and more active.

During weeks 25 and 26, the baby's brain is rapidly growing and developing, forming new neural connections. The baby can respond to light and dark, and may turn its head towards a source of light. The baby starts to develop more fat under the skin, which will help regulate body temperature after birth.
The baby's brain is rapidly growing and developing.

In weeks 23 and 24, the baby's skin is wrinkled and translucent, but will gradually become smoother as fat accumulates. The lungs develop more rapidly, although they are still immature and not fully ready for breathing outside the womb. The baby starts to gain more weight, preparing for the third trimester.

During weeks 21 and 22, the baby's movements increase and become more coordinated, with kicks and stretches becoming more noticeable. The baby starts to develop taste buds, which will allow the sense of taste to develop after birth. The baby is growing steadily and becoming more active.

During weeks 17 and 18, the baby can hear sounds from outside the womb and may respond with movements. The eyes can make slow movements as the baby starts to develop visual awareness. The skeleton is transitioning from soft cartilage to harder bone, providing more structure and strength.
The baby can hear sounds and may respond to them.

In weeks 19 and 20, the baby starts to develop a regular sleep pattern, alternating between periods of activity and rest. The baby may start to hiccup, which can sometimes be felt by the mother. A fine layer of hair called lanugo covers the baby's body, providing insulation and protection.

In weeks 15 and 16, the baby can suck its thumb and make breathing movements, although the lungs are not yet ready for air. The baby's skin develops, although it remains very thin and translucent. The baby is growing rapidly and becoming more coordinated in its movements.

During weeks 13 and 14, the baby can make facial expressions such as frowning or squinting. The bones start to harden, and hair begins to grow on the head. The baby is becoming more active and can even suck its thumb, a sign of developing motor skills.

In the twelfth week, the baby's organs are fully formed and begin to function independently. Fingernails and toenails start to develop, adding to the intricate details of the baby's anatomy. This marks the end of the first trimester, with the baby growing stronger and more active.

By the eleventh week, the baby's head is proportionally large, making up about half of its total body length. The skin is still very thin and translucent, allowing some internal structures to be visible. This period is critical for the rapid growth of the brain and body.

During the tenth week, the baby can make small, voluntary movements. Tooth buds form in the gums, which will later develop into baby teeth. The vital organs are continuing to mature, and the baby starts to resemble a tiny human.

In the ninth week, the baby's heart is fully developed and beating regularly. External genitalia begin to differentiate, although it is still too early to determine the baby's sex. The baby is now referred to as a fetus, and growth continues rapidly.

In the sixth week, the neural tube closes, and the brain begins to develop rapidly. Facial features such as eyes, ears, and the mouth start to take shape. These early developments are critical for the formation of the baby's head and facial structure.

By the eighth week, fingers and toes start to form, and the lungs begin to develop. These developments mark the transition from the embryonic stage to the fetal stage, where the body structures and organs become more defined.

During the fifth week, major organ systems start to form, including the heart, brain, and spinal cord. Limb buds also appear, which will eventually develop into the baby's arms and legs. This week marks the beginning of significant developmental changes.

In weeks 3 and 4, the embryonic disc forms, which will develop into the baby. The neural tube, the precursor to the central nervous system, starts to develop. By the end of this period, the heart begins to beat, marking one of the first vital signs of life.

During the first two weeks, fertilization occurs when the sperm fertilizes the egg, forming a zygote. The zygote then undergoes rapid cell division as it travels down the fallopian tube. By the end of the second week, the blastocyst implants itself into the uterine wall, beginning the crucial process of establishing the pregnancy.

During the seventh week, the heart continues to develop and becomes more complex, forming the chambers and valves that will be essential for circulation. The digestive system also begins to take shape, laying the groundwork for future nutrient absorption and digestion.
